A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FSM-based approach to vectorizing MCMC, with matching authors, core algorithms, theory and experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on delayed rejection, elliptical slice sampling, NUTS and transport elliptical slice sampling, including runtime, effective sample size and KSD results in Section 7 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental plots and reports additional NUTS comparisons in Section 7.4 and Appendix B.5, including results on Soil and Pilots.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's constructions for three specific loop patterns, v2 introduces an automated construction for arbitrary finite combinations of sequential and nested loops in a toy language: parsing, tree coarsening, recursive FSM assembly and empty-state removal (Appendix B.3, Algorithms 10–13). Algorithm 9 also adds a bundling procedure that stops when an amortized computation is required. These extend the construction and execution procedures while retaining the underlying MCMC kernels.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds the Soil and Pilots posterior targets from PosteriorDB. The earlier targets remain represented. Additional NUTS evaluations on Real-Estate GPR and the four Section 7.4 problems extend algorithm coverage on existing tasks rather than introducing further datasets.

E2.justification: In the corresponding four-problem comparison, v2 removes NeuTra and adds standard NUTS alongside its FSM implementation. MEADS, CHEES and the TESS comparison remain. NUTS already appeared in v1's separate mixture experiment, but its participation in this comparison is new.

E3.justification: Section 7.3 changes the stated mixture centers from (-5·1, 0, 5·1) to (-10·1, 0, 10·1), although Figure 7 is unchanged and does not establish that experiments were rerun. KSD is removed from the reported evaluation metrics. The added appendix NUTS comparisons specify 128 chains, 1000 samples and 400 warm-up steps for tuning.

E4.justification: The state-count/condensation, amortization, chain-count and dataset-size analyses retain their questions and plotted evidence. In particular, v1's supplementary Figures 8–9 reappear as v2's Figures 13 and 12. The additional NUTS tables provide benchmark comparisons without a new controlled ablation or robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 random seeds and standard deviations for delayed rejection and elliptical slice sampling, and five seeds with standard errors for the NUTS mixture experiment. The added tables introduce no new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 substantially expands NUTS results: Table 1 reports FSM speed-ups of 1.5×, 3.5×, 1.2× and 0.8× on the four retained problems; Appendix Table 2 adds 3.15× on Real-Estate GPR, 2.43× on Soil and 0.91× on Pilots. NeuTra results and all KSD entries from v1 disappear. Existing plotted results remain unchanged, and retained TESS results agree after rounding and conversion to ratios.

T1.justification: v2 adds an operator-based definition of the absolute spectral gap and explicit spectral-gap conditions in Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A, while removing v1's Remark 4.2. Section 2.2 replaces the law-of-large-numbers premise with a central-limit-theorem premise and probabilistic-order statements. The main efficiency bound and its proof remain substantially unchanged; Appendix B.3 additionally formalizes a program grammar.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contribution list retain the same central claims: FSM conversion avoids vectorization synchronization barriers, the simplified analysis supplies a speed-up bound and design recommendations, and implementations demonstrate speed-ups approaching an order of magnitude.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of NUTS slowdowns with cheap log densities and incomplete workload balancing after 1000 samples on Soil and Pilots. It also explains why ordinary bundling cannot directly accommodate intermediate amortized computations, and discusses potentially non-halting empty-state transitions in the generalized construction. These add specific applicability qualifications to the retained efficiency interpretation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and discloses that the implementation combines block execution and transition selection into composite functions handled by one switch. It also specifies precomputation requirements and details combined bundling/amortization. The A100 hardware, JAX/JIT implementation, 100-step scan blocks and compilation-time exclusions were already documented in v1.

R1.justification: v2 adds DeRemer (1969) for parsing and Magnusson et al. (2025) for PosteriorDB, while removing the NeuTra reference, Hoffman et al. (2019), and Rudolf (2011). The principal novelty positioning and comparison with Radul et al.'s batching approach remain substantively stable.

P1.justification: v2 edits and tightens prose, reorganizes Section 4 into separate long-run-cost and relative-cost subsections, expands implementation explanations, and adds an Impact Statement. Appendix B gains a structured construction walkthrough, but the main section sequence and much of the existing narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout, with extensive figure and algorithm reflow. Four new construction diagrams appear as Figures 8–11. Table 1 is redesigned around baseline ESS/sec and FSM speed-ups, and the appendix table is replaced. Existing plot images are retained, including reordered and renumbered experimental figures.

improvement.justification: v2 makes implementation more accessible through the generalized construction, combined bundling/amortization details and code link. Its additional NUTS evaluations strengthen evidence beyond the original synthetic example and expose useful limits, including slowdowns. These provide a modest net improvement, tempered by removal of NeuTra comparisons and all KSD diagnostics, which reduces comparative and sample-quality evidence. The main claims and original plotted results remain stable.
